Question: In baseball, since in some stadiums it is easier to hit home runs, do players who play half their games there have an unfair edge in the home run race?
Answer: Mel Ott played his entire career (1926-1947) for the New York Giants, whose home field was The Polo Grounds, a rectangular structure which was not well-suited to accomodate a baseball field. The left field wall was only 277 feet from home plate down the line, and the right field wall was even closer, at 256 feet. Question: In today's game, would you rather have a stud starting pitcher or a stud everyday player?
Answer: I will begin this answer by making the assumption that, for whichever player you do NOT choose, you get a completely average MLB full-time player to fill that slot. Since 1995 (an arbitrary cutoff perhaps, but I had to limit the amount of data I could work with) and through 2018, there were 3,623 batter-seasons which qualified for the batting title that year. The median batter had a WAR of 2.8; this serves as our baseline. Now we need to define “stud” — top 1%? Top 5%? Top 10%? The WARs provided by each of those cutoff points over that time period are 8.7, 6.9, and 5.9, or to be more meaningful, you got 5.9, 4.1, and 3.1 over an average full-time major league hitter. Now let’s do the same analysis for pitchers. There were 1,995 pitcher-seasons that qualified for the ERA title. The median WAR was 2.7 — almost identical to the median batter, because that is how the distribution is designed to work. A top 1% pitcher had a WAR of 8.6 (5.9 marginal value over the median); a top 5% pitcher had a WAR of 6.6 (3.9 marginal), and a top 10% pitcher had a WAR of 5.7 (3.0 marginal). So we have marginal WAR values of 5.9 vs. 5.9, 4.1 vs. 3.9, and 3.1 vs. 3.0 — a measure that favors stud hitters by an amount that is probably statistically insignificant. FYI, the single best seasons in that time frame — Bonds in 2001 and Clemens in 1997 — both resulted in WAR of 11.9.

Question: Would you rather your baseball team to have a player with a .275/.300/.600 or a .275/.400/.500 triple slash line?
Answer: One flawed assumption with the OPS statistic is that it assumes that on-base percentage and slugging average are equally important. Consider two batters — one who, in four plate appearances, hits three singles and makes one out, and the other hits two doubles and makes two outs. Each batter has an OPS of 1.500, but the first batter will produce 81 singles for every 27 outs (a full game), while the second batter will produce 27 doubles for every 27 outs. I think we would all agree that the 81 singles will most likely produce more runs. My conclusion is that, point-for-point, a high on-base percentage is more valuable than a high slugging average. I don’t know if SABR has done any extensive work on this, but there needs to be a calculation for a coefficient greater than 1 to be applied to the OBP component of the OPS calculation to improve its predictive value.

Question: What's the most lopsided trade in MLB history?

Another trade that turned out to be extremely profitable for one team was actually a series of trades made by the Pirates from 1973 to 1986. It went like this: December 1975: Pirates send catcher Milt May to the Astros for pitcher Jerry Reuss. May’s career WAR total after this trade was 13.8; Reuss’ was 28.1 April 1979: Pirates send Reuss to the Dodgers for pitcher Rick Rhoden. Reuss’ career WAR total after the trade was 19.2; Rhoden’s was 24.4 as a pitcher and another 4.1 as a batter (he was one of the best hitting pitchers of the 1980s) November 1986: Pirates send Rhoden and two others to the Yankees for Doug Drabek and two other players. Rhoden’s career WAR total after the trade was 4.0; Drabek’s was 26.1 and he won the Cy Young award in 1990. It was the gift that kept on giving.

Question: I have read so many articles about how much one will walk away if a person wins the big 1.73B Powerball. Which is more appropriate, lump sum or annuity distribution? Why?

Question: What was the most important play of the 1973 MLB regular season?
Answer: This is a strange question in that it feels like you are fishing for a particular answer. Well, let me give you that answer. On 20 September 1973 the Pirates were visiting the Mets, and after 12 innings the teams were tied 3–3. In the top of the 13th the Pirates had Richie Zisk on first base when Dave Augustine hit a long fly ball to left. The ball literally hit the top of the wall and bounced right back to Cleon Jones, who threw to Wayne Garrett, who relayed to Ron Hodges, who tagged Zisk out. The Mets pushed across a run in the bottom of the inning to win 4–3. If Zisk scores, not only do the Pirates have the lead but Augustine is in scoring position at second base to potentially add to the lead. When the season ended, the Mets were 82-79 (game 162 vs. the Cubs was not played), the Cardinals were 81-81, and the Pirates were 80-82. If the Pirates had won that game and the Mets lost game 162 to the Cubs, there would have been a three-way tie at 81-81.
